title: SpaceX Falcon 9 vehicle page
summary: SpaceX describes Falcon 9 as a reusable two-stage rocket and identifies major reusable-architecture elements including the first stage, Merlin engines, grid fins, landing legs, and fairing reuse.
excerpt: Falcon 9 is a reusable, two-stage rocket designed and manufactured by SpaceX for the reliable and safe transport of people and payloads into Earth orbit and beyond. Falcon 9 is the world's first orbital class reusable rocket. Falcon 9's first stage incorporates nine Merlin engines. Falcon 9 is equipped with four hypersonic grid fins positioned at the base of the interstage.
limitations: Real Falcon 9 page (JS-rendered; readable only via browser). Covers reusable stack, nine Merlin engines, grid fins; page also states landing legs, single Merlin Vacuum 2nd stage, and fairing recovery for reuse.

title: Falcon Payload User's Guide
summary: The 2025 Falcon payload guide documents fault-tolerant avionics/GNC, redundant/triplicated elements, upper-stage Merlin Vacuum, and payload integration interfaces.
excerpt: A single Merlin Vacuum (MVac) engine powers the second stage, using a fixed 165:1 expansion nozzle. Falcon launch vehicle avionics, and guidance, navigation, and control systems use a fault-tolerant architecture that provides full vehicle single-fault tolerance. The Falcon second stage ... use pneumatic devices that provide low-shock release and positive force separation.
limitations: Falcon User's Guide PDF (128pp). Verbatim quotes for single MVac fixed nozzle, fault-tolerant single-fault avionics/GNC, and pneumatic low-shock stage separation. Excerpt condenses three exact sentences (each individually verbatim).

title: NASA Crew-2 launch success and first reuse on a crew mission
summary: NASA reported Crew-2 as the first commercial crew mission to reuse both Crew Dragon and Falcon 9 rocket on a crew mission.
limitations: NASA Crew-2 blog loaded fine; verbatim line confirms first booster + Dragon reuse on a crewed Falcon 9 mission, supporting the operational-reuse claim.
excerpt: First reuse of the Crew Dragon spacecraft and Falcon 9 rocket on a crew mission –Crew Dragon Endeavour flew the historic Demo-2 mission and the Falcon 9 flew astronauts on the Crew-1 mission

title: SpaceX Starship vehicle page
summary: SpaceX describes Starship as designed to carry more than 100 metric tonnes to orbit in a fully reusable configuration.
limitations: Rendered page (JS SPA; plain fetch returned empty). Backs fully-reusable stack, ship upper stage, Super Heavy booster, 100t mass-to-orbit, payload bay. Page does NOT mention heat-shield tiles verbatim, so the tile sub-claim is unsupported by this URL (covered instead by the prospectus, p111).
excerpt: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy rocket - collectively referred to as Starship - represent a fully reusable transportation system designed to carry both crew and cargo to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond.

title: SpaceX EU prospectus / investor filing
summary: SpaceX investor filing describes the company's listing context, Starship/Super Heavy architecture claims, and AI compute ambition extending to space. It is used as issuer evidence, not as independent technical validation.
limitations: PDF (p110). Single sentence backs Super Heavy reusable booster, 33-Raptor cluster, sea-level+vacuum Raptor mix, Starship/Super Heavy reusable branch, mass-to-orbit. excerpt: Comprising the Super Heavy booster (powered by 33 Raptor engines) and the Starship upper stage (with three sea-level and three vacuum Raptor engines), Starship V3 is designed to deliver 100 metric tons to space in a fully reusable configuration

title: FAA Starship / Super Heavy Boca Chica project page

title: FCC public notice accepting SpaceX Orbital Data Center system application
summary: FCC notice says SpaceX filed on January 30, 2026 for authority to launch and operate a new NGSO system of up to one million satellites as the SpaceX Orbital Data Center system, primarily relying on optical inter-satellite links and possible Starlink interconnection.
limitations: PDF (DA 26-113, Feb 4 2026). Backs orbital data center system (accepted-for-filing, NGSO up to 1M sats), optical ISL fabric, TT&C layer, Starlink Gen1/Gen2 interconnect, and license/waiver status (milestone/deployment & surety-bond waiver requests = public-notice stage, not commercial deployment).
excerpt: The proposed satellites will use high-bandwidth optical inter-satellite links and conduct telemetry, tracking, and command (TT&C) operations.

title: Starlink Technology page: space lasers / optical ISLs
summary: Starlink describes optical inter-satellite links / space lasers as a high-bandwidth space network technology. Used as evidence for Starlink optical-network dependency, not for orbital compute maturity.
limitations: Rendered page (JS SPA; plain fetch returned empty). Backs optical ISL network fabric and laser-terminal backhaul (200 Gbps). Latency/bandwidth sub-claim also backed: 'latency is significantly lower-around 25 ms vs 600+ ms.'
excerpt: Each Starlink satellite contains 3 space lasers (Optical Intersatellite Links or ISLs) operating at up to 200 Gbps, which together across the constellation form a global internet mesh that can connect customers anywhere in the world.

title: NASA Small Spacecraft Technology: thermal control
summary: NASA thermal-control chapter explains spacecraft heat balance, thermal radiation, passive/active thermal technologies, deployable radiators, heat pipes, coatings, and small spacecraft thermal constraints.
limitations: Backs orbital thermal rejection (radiate-only constraint), deployable radiator panels, heat-pipe transport, and coating degradation ('Coatings will darken due to atomic oxygen bombardment ... This will increase the solar absorptance values'). No verbatim TVAC-test sentence on page; that sub-claim is the weakest fit but core thermal claims hold.
excerpt: In a vacuum, heat is transferred only by radiation and conduction with no convection. A deployable radiator is stowed during transit or when the radiator is not needed and deployed when excess heat dissipation is required.

title: NASA NEPP radiation effects primer
summary: NASA NEPP material explains radiation effects such as total ionizing dose and single-event effects. Used for radiation-risk logic in orbital compute electronics.
limitations: PDF slide deck (NASA NEPP 'Radiation Effects 101'). Backs SEE/SEU/SEL/latchup watchdog-recovery, TID shielding ('Total Ionizing Dose (TID) ... Can partially mitigate with shielding'), ECC/data-integrity ('error detection and correction (EDAC) on large memory arrays'), parts selection (RHA), and ground radiation test campaign ('All devices with unknown characteristics should be ground radiation tested (TID and SEE)').
excerpt: Single Event Latchup (SEL) - a condition which causes loss of device functionality due to a single event induced high current state. An SEL may or may not cause permanent device damage, but requires power strobing of the device to resume normal device operation.

title: NASA Kennedy Space Shuttle Orbiter Thermal Protection System
summary: NASA Kennedy's thermal-protection-system brief describes reusable tile inspection and repair after missions, average tile replacement, silicone adhesive tile bonding to strain-isolator pads, gap control, gap fillers, and rewaterproofing. It supports the bottleneck logic that reusable tile TPS is a maintenance, bonding, inspection, and turnaround process rather than just a material.
limitations: NASA Kennedy Orbiter TPS PDF (8pp). Verbatim quotes for reusable tiles, per-mission tile replacement (~50), tile bonding/attachment via silicone adhesive + strain isolator, and inspection process — backs heat-shield-tile durability/bonding/inspection bottleneck claims.
excerpt: An average of 50 tiles are replaced after each mission, either due to handling damage or accumulated repairs. The tiles are bonded to the orbiter with a silicone adhesive. The tiles are first bonded to a strain isolator pad. ... a light-weight, reusable thermal protection system composed of entirely new materials.
